items.title: South Korean lasers down three drones in Army demo, Hanwha says
items.originalTitle: South Korean lasers down three drones in Army demo, Hanwha says
items.summary: Two laser weapons developed by Hanwha Systems shot down all three target drones during a South Korean Army demonstration on Oct. 14, the company said, as it pitches the technology to foreign buyers. The company’s stationary Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt-class vehicle-mounted laser took part in the live-fire event, held during the Army’s TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise. About 500 people attended, according to Hanwha, including Army Chief of Staff Gen.

evidenceRecords.text: Two laser weapons developed by Hanwha Systems shot down all three target drones during a South Korean Army demonstration on Oct. 14, the company said, as it pitches the technology to foreign buyers.

The company’s stationary Cheongwang laser air defense weapon and a 30-kilowatt-class vehicle-mounted laser took part in the live-fire event, held during the Army’s TIGER+ Future Warfare Integrated Combat Exercise.
About 500 people attended, according to Hanwha, including Army Chief of Staff Gen.
Cheongwang fired on a drone overhead that “caught fire and fell from the sky,” The Korea Times reported from the exercise at a training ground in Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi Province.
The laser was one part of a layered counter-drone demonstration that also included electronic jamming and a K21 armored vehicle firing on incoming drones.
Hanwha did not say which system destroyed which drones, what kinds of drones were used, what vehicle carries the newer laser or the range of either weapon.

The Oct. 14 demonstration followed a Sept. 16 event at South Korea’s 2026 Defense Drone Technology Exhibition, where Cheongwang downed four drones and two larger unmanned aircraft in succession, Hanwha said.
Cheongwang, meaning “light of the sky,” in Korean is formally known as the Laser Air Defense Weapon Block-I.
Hanwha developed it under a program led by South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development.
The company calls it the world’s first operationally deployed laser weapon.

South Korea first fielded the system in December 2024 and had about five units at major government facilities as of June, including the Ministry of National Defense building, according to Korea JoongAng Daily .
North Korean drones have repeatedly violated South Korean airspace.

April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast.
The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon.
As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowd’s voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet.
For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible.
For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget.
That moment also offered a pause for reflection on the work that led her there.
As the spacecraft offline operations manager, Mjoen coordinates the work that happens long before launch day.

By supporting the ground systems’ senior vehicle operations manager, Matt Czech, she develops integration plans and oversees ground operations for Artemis vehicle processing, focusing on booster and Orion spacecraft operations.
Mjoen began her career as a flight crew systems engineer with United Space Alliance supporting the Space Shuttle Program.

The system uses a concentrated beam of light instead of costly missile interceptors, potentially offering a less expensive way to bring down drones.
The pilot program will place directed-energy weapons at military bases across the country for a yearlong assessment, where service members will operate, maintain and collect data on the weapons.
The Pentagon will, in turn, gather information on cost and logistics.
KBR subsidiary Kord has marketed Firefly as a palletized mobile laser.
The company said the system — part of which looks like a futuristic, modular cell phone camera lens — can operate in temperatures ranging from negative 15 to 35 degrees Celsius.
During an August demonstration in Alabama, company officials said that a truck-mounted system needs just a few seconds to down a small drone.

items.originalTitle: Blue Origin to add new Florida launch pads, seeks aggressive increase in New Glenn flight rate
items.summary: Graphic: Blue Origin Blue Origin said it will add new launch pads on Florida’s Space Coast to help ramp up the flight rate of its New Glenn rockets, as the company recovers from a catastrophic test fire explosion in May. In a series of other infrastructure announcements Friday morning, Ian Richardson, the Senior Vice President of Operations at Blue Origin, said the company was serious about launching and landing more rockets.

evidenceRecords.text: Graphic: Blue Origin Blue Origin said it will add new launch pads on Florida’s Space Coast to help ramp up the flight rate of its New Glenn rockets, as the company recovers from a catastrophic test fire explosion in May.

In a series of other infrastructure announcements Friday morning, Ian Richardson, the Senior Vice President of Operations at Blue Origin, said the company was serious about launching and landing more rockets.

“As we look ahead, this infrastructure is designed to support multiple flights per week by the end of the decade.” The new pads would be modeled after Blue Origin facilities at Launch Complex 36 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.

LC-36A, which is being rebuilt after the static test fire explosion, serves the New Glenn 7×2 rocket and LC-36B is under construction to support launches of the 9×4 variant of the rocket, which features nine BE-4 engines on the first stage and four BE-3U engines on the upper stage.

Spectators along the beach in Cape Canaveral, Florida, enjoy a spectacular Sunday morning launch, taking in the view of a Blue Origin New Glenn rocket blasting off carrying a next-generation cellular broadband satellite.
The company said later the AST SpaceMobile Bluebird 7 satellite ended up in the wrong orbit.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the middle of a 30-day comment period as it seeks public input on Blue Origin’s request to increase its launch cadence at LC-36A from 12 permitted flights up to 50.
A virtual public hearing is scheduled for Thursday, Oct. 22, and public comment closes on Oct. 30.
With more pads coming online, Blue Origin said it will also introduce two new landing vessels to its marine fleet.
Simultaneously, a payload processing facility that can be used by both Blue Origin and others is being built in partnership with the U.S. Space Force.
A payload processing facility is shown under construction at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.
The facility is being built by Blue Origin with support from the U.S. Space Force.

The next threat that we see to get in front of is the jet-powered Shahed drones,” Brett Velicovich, cofounder and president of the dronemaker Powerus, told Defense One .
“Jet-powered Shaheds are very difficult to defeat because of how fast they are, and so to defeat those, we need jet-powered interceptors.

There's a good chance that by the end of this year, the majority of Russian drones that are sent into downtown Kyiv will be jet-powered,” he said, “so we really need to move at that timeline.” But churning out rocket- or jet-propelled interceptors at the same rate as the upgraded Shahed drones can be costly and difficult.

Newer versions of Shahed drones propelled by jet engines have increasingly been appearing on the Russian-Ukrainian battlefield in recent months, pushing Ukraine to fortify its air defenses.
Those fast flying Shaheds require interceptors that can match those speeds\u2014around 370 mph, or 600 kilometers per hour.
Other versions of the Shahed fly just over 100 mph.
There\u2019s also concern that other security risks could crop up as other nations adopt the newer Shaheds.\u00a0
Powerus is just about a year old and has former Pentagon and first Trump administration officials on its board.
Velicovich doesn\u2019t have a target date for developing its rocket or jet-powered interceptor, but the goal is to move quickly.\u00a0

items.originalTitle: Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House, sources say
items.summary: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed. The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order.

evidenceRecords.text: The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
The officials said leaders at the Defense Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order.
The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.

Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of ‌Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.

U.S. pressures Ukraine over refinery attacks The move to temporarily restrict the vital communications system came as President Donald Trump has pressured Kyiv to stop its attacks on Russian refineries, which he has blamed for the soaring energy prices that are denting his Republican Party’s prospects in the November midterm elections.

In response to a request for comment about the order to limit Starshield, a senior U.S. official said: “No such request was ever made by the president.” The White House did not respond to questions about whether other administration officials might have made the request.
Starshield was developed by SpaceX specifically for government and national-security customers, particularly the U.S. Department of Defense.
Starshield uses the Starlink constellation as its backbone.

Ukrainian officials said the restrictions complicated strike missions against Russian forces and logistics in occupied territory and slowed interceptor drones used to shoot down incoming Russian Shahed drones.

Following the move to restrict Ukraine’s access to Starshield, the Ukrainians made calls on Tuesday and Wednesday to find answers from senior officials at the White House, State Department and Pentagon, a senior Ukrainian official said, adding that Kyiv was told it was a White House decision.
The Pentagon has spent billions of dollars on the Starlink and Starshield services.

items.summary: Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defenses after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday. Drones hit two ships that caught fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.

evidenceRecords.text: Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to bolster its defenses after a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday.
Drones hit two ships that caught fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast this week.
On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast following a drone attack, prompting Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.

The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to commercial shipping near NATO’s southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defenses in the Black Sea.

“We have sent letters and a request to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory.
Stoyanov said he planned to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Thursday, saying afterwards that NATO would “continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed.” Asked about Bulgaria’s request on Friday, a NATO official said the issue would be discussed further by ambassadors from the alliance’s 32 member states next week.
Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October.

items.originalTitle: Lockheed invests $300M in Texas plant to feed missile surge
items.summary: Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile. The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama. Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin is investing $300 million to expand its plant in Grand Prairie, Texas, which supports all programs across its Missiles and Fire Control business, including the PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptors, the Precision Strike Missile and the AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.
The company said Oct. 14 that the expansion will help the plant reach record production levels and deliver components to final-assembly sites, including Camden, Arkansas and Troy, Alabama.
Nearly 800 production employees work at the plant, which produced 250,000 parts in 2025.
Lockheed said it has added more than 30 high-precision machines in recent months and expects to install nearly 100 additional machines by the end of 2026.
Lockheed also said Hadrian, a California-based manufacturing startup, will install 24 automated machines at the Grand Prairie facility to produce missile parts.
Lockheed employees will operate the equipment, which is expected to be up and running by early 2027.
The project follows a memorandum of understanding the two companies signed in December 2025.
The buildout supports a series of framework agreements the Defense Department has signed with Lockheed since January, designed to boost missile production and lead to long-term contracts.
The first aims to increase PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to roughly 2,000 interceptors per year over seven years.
A separate THAAD framework, signed in January, led to a June contract from the Missile Defense Agency worth more than $35 billion to quadruple interceptor production.
Lockheed and the Pentagon announced similar agreements for the Precision Strike Missile on March 25 and for the AIM-260 on Sept. 17.

“Lockheed Martin has brought together commercial speed and combat-proven performance because America needs both,” said Jim Taiclet, Lockheed’s chairman, president and CEO. “By combining advanced technology with the expertise of our American workforce, we’re transforming manufacturing to deliver critical munitions at speed and scale.”

The fact that we have also been able to develop and test the system in such a short timeframe demonstrates the strength of the collaboration between the Swedish Armed Forces, FMV and Saab,” says Mats Wicksell, head of Saab’s business area Naval.
The LUUV project builds on Saab’s earlier investments and work in autonomous underwater systems and is now led by FMV in cooperation with the Swedish Armed Forces and Saab.
Developed at pace and according to plan, the demonstrator has progressed from concept to a fully functional vehicle.
Following successful sea trials, the first phase of the project has been completed.
The next phase is expected to focus on developing more advanced capabilities.
The results will support the continued development of software, sensors and autonomous functions, while also contributing to future product development.
The vehicle illustrates how close collaboration between industry and government authorities can significantly reduce the time from identifying an operational need to testing a new capability.
“This project demonstrates how new technologies can be rapidly translated into practical operational value.
The uncrewed underwater vehicle can contribute to increased endurance, enhanced situational awareness and strengthened underwater capabilities.
The demonstrator has been developed to support the development and evaluation of future underwater capabilities and to enable operations alongside existing naval platforms, such as submarines.

The rapid development has been enabled by Saab’s software-centric approach and the integration of Autonomous Ocean Core, Saab’s autonomous control system that provides surface and subsurface vehicles with autonomous capabilities.
Combined with Swedish expertise in submarine design and sensor integration, this has made it possible to take the project swiftly from concept to sea trials.

The CFFI would make use of Lydd’s existing aviation infrastructure and surrounding airspace, with a focus on technologies including uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS), advanced air mobility, autonomous systems and green propulsion technologies, said the airport in a press release.
Sam O’Dwyer, Chief Executive of Lydd Airport, said: “The demand to design, test and build new air systems at scale in the UK already exists, but it won’t wait indefinitely.
Other European countries are moving quicker and the UK, a global player in aviation innovation, risks falling behind.
Our ambition is for Lydd to become the UK’s Centre for Future Flight Innovation.
In partnership with Eagle Eye Innovations, we have developed a roadmap to foster innovation in drones and other new technologies through safe, secure and innovative operations.

Lydd can also provide a blueprint for other regional airports, repurposing existing infrastructure and professional capability to drive growth, attract investment and strengthen national capability.” Eagle Eye Innovations is one of the industry partners supporting the CFFI and has worked with Lydd Airport on the roadmap and strategic vision for the Centre.

items.summary: The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.” Although the Cheyenne being equipped with over double the speed and range of current weapons systems will be transformative, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software, Frank Lazzara, Bell’s director of MV-75 Sales & Strategy, told Military Times in an interview.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne II is expected to bring increased capability to the service, not just through its boosted speed and range but also with its “digital backbone.” Although the Cheyenne being equipped with over double the speed and range of current weapons systems will be transformative, Bell, the defense manufacturer for the aircraft, anticipates the real “revolutionary” part to be its software, Frank Lazzara, Bell’s director of MV-75 Sales & Strategy, told Military Times in an interview.

The Cheyenne program is the service’s inaugural “digital-first” weapons system with a modular open systems approach , or MOSA, that allows the Army to virtually refine its architecture and helps acquire intellectual property and data rights needed to control future upgrades and avoid vendor lock-in.

“The Army is trying to set the standard for the government to have control over their maintenance, their upgradeability, like they’ve never had before,” Lazzara said at the 2026 Association of the United States Army conference in Washington, D.C.

Bell’s open system approach differs from others, he said, because it is guided and directed by the Army, giving them more control and changing the way business is conducted throughout the lifecycle of the aircraft.
“This is the model for what the government should get when they acquire a weapon system of this level and an acquisition at this level,” Lazzara said.

“That’s what gets lost out there.” “You can hang another system on an old aircraft, and you might have a little bit more capability, but you’re never going to have the capability you have in this aircraft, plus the ability to much more easily upgrade and maintain your aircraft through its life cycle,” he continued.

“That’s where the payoff really happens.” The Cheyenne , which is designed to be a multi-mission aircraft, is the Army’s next-generation tiltrotor assault and utility aircraft, slated to replace part of the force’s UH-60 Black Hawk fleet.

items.title: Former defence minister Fedorov announces Ukrainian interceptor test to counter high-speed drones
items.originalTitle: Former defence minister Fedorov announces Ukrainian interceptor test to counter high-speed drones
items.summary: Ukraine’s former defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, who was credited with modernising the country’s drone and counter-drone capabilities in the face of Russian attacks, is developing a new drone interceptor. Currently flown by a human pilot, Fedorov and his engineering team are developing the system to fly autonomously at high speeds with the assistance of artificial intelligence. According to Fedorov’s LinkedIn post, the interceptor was recently subject to testing by Lasar’s Group, in which it took down two Geran-5 jet-powered drones.

items.summary: Fincantieri has cut steel for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) at its Riva Trigoso shipyard, marking the start of construction on the Italian Navy’s final PPA vessel. On October 15, 2026, the First Steel Cutting Ceremony for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) was held at Fincantieri’s integrated shipyard in Riva Trigoso, officially marking the commencement of construction of the vessel and a significant milestone for the Programme.

OCCAR press release On October 15, 2026, the First Steel Cutting Ceremony for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) was held at Fincantieri’s integrated shipyard in Riva Trigoso, officially marking the commencement of construction of the vessel and a significant milestone for the Programme.
The ceremony represents the formal launch of production activities for the ninth unit of the PPA Class, which will become the seventh and final ship delivered to the Italian Navy under the Programme.

In accordance with established shipbuilding tradition, the laser cutting machine was ceremonially activated by representatives of the Italian Navy, acting as Customer, OCCAR as Contracting Authority, and FINCANTIERI as Prime Contractor.

As the seventh and final unit to be delivered under the Programme, PPA 9 represents the culmination of a significant naval procurement initiative, providing the Italian Navy with a highly capable, flexible and technologically advanced platform designed to meet current and future operational requirements. – End –

On October 15, 2026, the First Steel Cutting Ceremony for the ninth Multipurpose Patrol Ship (PPA 9) was held at Fincantieri’s integrated shipyard in Riva Trigoso, officially marking the commencement of construction of the vessel and a significant milestone for the Programme.
The event marked the first physical stage in the construction process and underscored the continued cooperation between all Programme stakeholders.
Following Contract Amendment No. 10, PPA 9 will be constructed in the Full Combat Configuration, the most advanced and capable variant of the class.

Designed to conduct operations across the full spectrum of maritime missions and principal warfare domains, the vessel will incorporate enhanced combat system capabilities to ensure the highest standards of operational readiness, survivability and mission effectiveness.
The commencement of construction of PPA 9 demonstrates the continued progress and maturity of the Programme, which remains a cornerstone of the Italian Navy’s fleet renewal effort.
To date, five of the seven vessels contracted for delivery to the Marina Militare Italiana, the Italian Navy have entered service, while the sixth unit, PPA 8, is currently under construction.

As the seventh and final unit to be delivered under the Programme, PPA 9 represents the culmination of a significant naval procurement initiative, providing the Italian Navy with a highly capable, flexible and technologically advanced platform designed to meet current and future operational requirements.

evidenceRecords.text: To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process.

The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations.
The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance.
The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref.
Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness.
The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref.

One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar).
Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process.

“Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app.
After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.
After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.

COMSOL A “Tool Within a Tool” for Busbar Weld Design The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles.

items.summary: Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks. evidenceRecords.text: Attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the latest fighting between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks.
The attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the current conflict between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
The palace is the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government.

Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks.
Yemen’s prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, ⁠and cabinet members were safe following the attack, Yemeni information minister Moammar al-Eryani said.
Witnesses told Reuters they heard loud booms near the palace.
Yemen’s cabinet said the attack involved missiles and drones.
Yemen’s health minister, Qasim Buhaibeh, said five people were killed and 16 wounded in the attack, with casualties including guards and civilian employees.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said its fighters had bombed what he described as ​the Saudi military operations headquarters in Aden, as part of the group’s declared policy ‌of targeting “Saudi reinforcements wherever they were located”.
Agence France-Presse reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity that the palace attack had hit a command centre for the Saudi-led coalition.

The official added that the command centre was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

Fighting has escalated between the Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition as part of clashes linked to the US and Israeli war on Iran, and aid agencies have warned of rapidly worsening conditions in Yemen.
The clashes have complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks.

Why radar and AIS leave a gap in maritime domain awareness SEA.AI picture Radar resolves a contact’s position and radar cross-section, but not what the contact is.
SEA.AI’s machine vision, that classifies contacts autonomously and in real time, is a direct solution for closing a real gap.
That is why it is on our platforms.” Jim HarveyChief Technology Officer, MARTAC SEA.AI machine vision, proven at sea since 2018 SEA.AI pioneered maritime machine vision in 2018.
MARTAC has integrated SEA.AI maritime machine vision on its unmanned surface vessels (USVs).
The integration covers ISR, security, and patrol mission profiles.

In today’s grey zone environment, these limits carry operational weight because threats are designed to exploit them: dark vessels, spoofed identities, and fast-attack craft that look like surrounding traffic until the moment they act.
Electro-optical and thermal cameras have long been part of maritime sensing.
The weak point is what happens after the image is captured.
On an autonomous platform, a conventional camera produces video, and that video is useless without an analyst watching it continuously.
SEA.AI runs AI inference at the sensor level.

Brazil has spent years building a regulatory framework for drones.
In June 2026, it took another significant step, replacing its previous rules with a new risk-based system designed to accommodate a wider range of civil uncrewed aircraft system (UAS) operations.1
But regulation is only one part of integrating drones into the airspace; enforcing those regulations is the other.
What happens when operators do not follow the rules?
Do authorities have the tools and coordination needed to respond?
Brazil is now dealing with both sides of that equation.
In June 2026, Brazil’s national civil aviation agency, Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (ANAC), approved RBAC 100, replacing the previous RBAC-E 94 framework.
The new regulation moved away from a system primarily based on drone weight and introduced three categories based on the risk of the operation: open, specific and certified.1

The open category covers lower risk operations, including flights of aircraft weighing up to 25 kg, within visual or extended visual line of sight and up to 120 metres above ground level, subject to defined conditions.

Operations that do not meet the requirements of the open category fall into the specific category and require either compliance with a standard scenario established by ANAC or an operational authorisation based on a risk assessment.

ANAC’s regulatory analysis identified the consolidation of the UAS market and the need for requirements covering areas including airworthiness, operations, maintenance, training, pilot qualifications and registration.
It also proposed a performance-based approach intended to provide greater flexibility as technology and applications develop.2

The airport was selected in part because of its history of drone incidents, highlighting the need to move beyond defining the rules towards developing the capabilities needed when those rules are not followed.4

items.originalTitle: NASA to Help Unlock Mysteries of Mars’ Moons in Upcoming Mission
items.summary: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet. The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth. The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

“The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanity’s understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.”
Scientists have long debated the origin of Mars’ two moons.
The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

“Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity billions of years ago,” said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.”
Another key part of NASA’s contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA.

NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moon’s origin and the evolution of the Mars system.

evidenceRecords.text: ANKARA — Turkish Aerospace has completed construction of a second production line for its Anka 3 unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) that is scheduled to open in November, a company official told Breaking Defense.

The new production line will manufacture a new variant of the Anka 3 drone that features a larger airframe and an expected payload capacity of 1.75 tons, up from about 1.3 tons on the original platform.
According to the Turkish Aerospace official, the upgraded aircraft will be able to carry more munitions to meet new national requirements.
During a visit to the company’s Ankara facility on Wednesday, the official said the first aircraft to be built on the new line is expected to roll out “soon” and undergo flight testing afterward.
The Anka 3 is a combat drone designed for strike and other missions.
The aircraft can reach high-subsonic speeds and operate at altitudes of up to 40,000 feet, according to Turkish Aerospace.
The Turkish armed forces ordered 80 Anka 3 UCAVs, with first delivery expected in 2027.
Media were invited to cover Atış Serbest exercise in Turkey and tour facilities of five defense firms: Aselsan, Turkish Aerospace, Asfat, MKE and Roketsan.
Breaking Defense accepted travel and accommodation from Turkish Ministry of Defense.
During the media tour, reporters had a closer look at the first prototype of the original Anka 3 drone, which is currently in flight testing.
In the same hangar, eight Anka medium-altitude long-endurance (MALE) UAVs were on display at different stages of the final assembly process.
Some were missing their fixed wings, while others were seen without parts of their fuselages.
A ninth Anka was being prepared for test flights, according to the company official.

items.title: Terra Quantum Joins QuEra Quantum Alliance
items.originalTitle: Terra Quantum Joins QuEra Quantum Alliance
items.summary: Insider Brief Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, adding its quantum software, algorithms and enterprise application expertise to the neutral-atom quantum computing partner network. Terra Quantum ‘s TQ42 platform provides a cloud-based quantum software environment with a Python SDK, APIs and algorithms for optimization, quantum machine learning and simulation. The partnership aims to connect enterprise applications with QuEra’s neutral-atom hardware, as QuEra targets availability of its 256-logical-qubit Libra fault-tolerant quantum computer through Amazon Braket in 2028.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, adding its quantum software, algorithms and enterprise application expertise to the neutral-atom quantum computing partner network.
Terra Quantum ‘s TQ42 platform provides a cloud-based quantum software environment with a Python SDK, APIs and algorithms for optimization, quantum machine learning and simulation.

The partnership aims to connect enterprise applications with QuEra’s neutral-atom hardware, as QuEra targets availability of its 256-logical-qubit Libra fault-tolerant quantum computer through Amazon Braket in 2028.

PRESS RELEASE — Terra Quantum , a global leader in the development of quantum technologies and their industrial application, the leader in neutral-atom quantum computing, today announced that Terra Quantum has joined the QuEra Quantum Alliance, a global partner program dedicated to accelerating the development, deployment, and utilization of neutral-atom quantum computers to solve the world’s most challenging computational problems.
Reinforcing the Applications Layer of the QuEra Quantum Alliance Terra Quantum is hardware-agnostic by design, developing proprietary algorithms and software rather than quantum processors.

As a member of the QuEra Quantum Alliance, Terra Quantum will gain access to technical expertise and go-to-market resources from QuEra as well as partnership opportunities with other, complementary alliance members.
Both QuEra and Terra Quantum see their expanded partnership as an opportunity to shorten the distance between an enterprise use case and hardware designed to scale toward fault tolerance.
“Quantum computing will create its real economic impact when world-class hardware and world-class applications come together,” said Markus Pflitsch, Founder, Chairman and CEO of Terra Quantum .

By joining the QuEra Quantum Alliance, we are bringing our algorithms and application expertise closer to one of the most promising hardware platforms in the industry, helping turn advances in quantum computing into solutions for real-world problems.” A Growing Global Alliance The QuEra Quantum Alliance brings together quantum hardware, software, and service providers to foster collaboration and widespread adoption of neutral-atom quantum computing.
Terra Quantum joins in a year when QuEra has put a dated path to fault tolerance on the record.

Libra , QuEra’s first fault-tolerant quantum computer, is a 256 logical qubit, megaquop-class system targeted for availability on Amazon Braket in 2028, and QuEra has since detailed a next-generation gigaquop-class FTQC system.

“ Terra Quantum strengthens the software and applications layer of the QuEra Quantum Alliance, which is where most enterprise conversations actually begin,” said Yuval Boger, Chief Commercial Officer at QuEra Computing.

Jaysen Yochim, Senior Director for the ALC program at Airbus, talked about the demonstration for the Army with our Howard Altman at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention on Monday.
Airbus is currently teamed with L3Harris Technologies, Shield AI, and Parry Labs on development of this drone helicopter for the Marines, as you can learn more about here .
The current iteration of the MQ-72C is based on the crewed UH-72B Lakota, which is in turn a variant of Airbus’ H145 twin-engine light helicopter.
The Army operates crewed UH-72s today , but only in non-combat roles, including counter-drug and border patrol missions, and almost exclusively within the borders of the United States.
US Army crewed UH-72 Lakota helicopters.
US Army The MQ-72C demonstration for the Army, which Airbus self-funded, took place last week at Huntsville Executive Airport just outside of Huntsville, Alabama.

“We did multiple traffic patterns to demonstrate just a normal traffic pattern, like a normal day would be, but also traffic patterns or a flight with a no-fly zone popping up in the middle of the flight.” The video below shows previous flight testing of the MQ-72C demonstrator.
In that latter instance, the MQ-72C had to “autonomously make decisions” about how it was “going to route itself around the no-fly zones” once they popped up, he added.
Though the demonstrator now has provisions for a pilot, the intention is for the MQ-72C to eventually operate in a completely uncrewed mode.

items.originalTitle: Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable
items.summary: As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian. Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

evidenceRecords.text: Kremlin turning to punishment of Ukraine’s population in major cities as frontlines remain frozen Europe live – latest updates As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.

Even as Donald Trump unilaterally declared an “energy ceasefire” last week between Moscow and Kyiv, Russia continued with its methodical and devastating strikes on Ukraine’s power grid, in particular in Kyiv, in a strategy meant to punish Ukraine’s population and drive the country to capitulation.

As Russian missiles and drones have systematically slammed into power plants in Kyiv and Kharkiv this week, the rolling blackouts and water outages have increasingly resembled a supposed Russian blueprint to destroy life in major Ukrainian cities seen by the Guardian.

The potential goals of the Russian campaign, according to an assessment seen by the Guardian that Ukrainian intelligence said it intercepted from Russia last month, range from “degrading the quality of life” of Ukrainians through power outages to fully shutting off the water supply, which the document cooly predicts would cause the “deterioration of sanitary conditions and the forced outflow of residents from cities.”

The document does not specify which Russian agency developed the assessment, which is titled Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy, Housing and Utilities Sectors, includes vulnerable Ukrainian energy grid targets and even contemplates strikes against high-risk sites, including the switchyards at several nuclear power plants.

But several European officials familiar with the document have said it is likely to have been produced by analytical departments linked to the Russian military or intelligence agencies, and that copies have circulated in Ukraine in previous years.

On Tuesday night, Russian strikes hit three major power plants in the Kyiv region – Combined Heat and Power Plants 4 and 5, and the Trypillya Thermal Power Plant in the Kyiv region – as well as a major electrical substation that transfers electricity from two of the country’s main nuclear power plants to the capital.

Those, along with other substations that make up the “Kyiv energy ring” that helps bring electricity from across the country to the capital, have all been targets of a Russian barrage that, if it succeeds, could threaten a humanitarian catastrophe in a city of 3 million people.

items.summary: Spanish air navigation services provider ENAIRE, the Benidorm City Council and the Polytechnic University of Valencia met on 15 October to discuss U-space in Benidorm. ENAIRE also provided an uncrewed traffic management demonstration. The meeting was held with the intention of bringing administrations, operators, users and agents of the sector closer to the safe and efficient integration of drones in the airspace.

evidenceRecords.text: Spanish air navigation services provider ENAIRE, the Benidorm City Council and the Polytechnic University of Valencia met on 15 October to discuss U-space in Benidorm.
For more information ENAIRE The post ENAIRE and partners discuss next steps for U-space in Benidorm first appeared on Unmanned airspace .
ENAIRE also provided an uncrewed traffic management demonstration.
The meeting was held with the intention of bringing administrations, operators, users and agents of the sector closer to the safe and efficient integration of drones in the airspace.

Institutional representatives and national and international experts analysed the current state of U-space services, the European regulatory framework and the new opportunities opened up by the operation of uncrewed aircraft in urban environments.

During the morning, EUROCONTROL specialists presented the evolution of the U-space project in Europe, while representatives of the Directorate General of Civil Aviation presented the progress of the National Action Plan for the Deployment of U-space and zoning (2026-2030 (PANDU+), an initiative aimed at facilitating the coordinated deployment of these services.
ENAIRE and the Polytechnic University of Valencia discussed the implications of U-space for drone operators and manned aviation.

The session addressed key aspects such as new operating procedures, safety benefits, requirements for UAS operations, available aeronautical information and the role of the Geozone Manager in airspace management.
ENAIRE presented a practical simulation of the U-space services through a demonstration of the digital platform that enables the safe and coordinated management of drone operations.
Attendees were able to experience processes such as flight plan activation, automated alert management and interaction with dynamic geographic areas.
Benidorm has a growing role as a laboratory for the development of advanced air mobility in Europe.

In February 2025, Benidorm hosted the first simultaneous operation in Europe involving an uncrewed air taxi and multiple drones in an urban environment managed through U-space services under the European U-ELCOME project.

ENAIRE said that yesterday’s event detailed how the progress demonstrated in that project is being progressively transferred from the experimental to the operational level, bringing administrations, operators and citizens closer to the capabilities that will make the safe expansion of drone operations possible in the cities of the future.

evidenceRecords.text: Google Deepmind's Gemini 4 Argon scored 97.5 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, making Google the second lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark.
The article Google's Gemini 4 Argon is closer to the AI frontier than any Google model in months appeared first on The Decoder .

Google Deepmind's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, scored 97.5 percent on ARC-AGI-3 at a cost of $4,800 using the "Provider Adapter Harness," a test setup that uses vendor-specific features like retained reasoning and context compaction.
According to ARC Prize, Google is now the second AI lab after OpenAI to cross the 95 percent mark on what is widely considered the toughest benchmark for general problem-solving.
Only GPT-6 Astra scores higher at 99.9 percent.
Like Astra, Argon needed 62 percent fewer actions than the human baseline across the 25 public games.
It matched or beat the speedrun record in three games and came within 10 percent of the best time in six others.

On older versions of the benchmark, Argon scored 91.3 percent on ARC-AGI-2 ($0.32 per task) and 98.5 percent on ARC-AGI-1 ($0.16 per task), based on the introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens.
In the "Standard Harness," which only allows simple notes between rounds, Argon drops to 49.8 percent at low reasoning for $5,800.
This gap traces back to a July 2026 dispute when OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol beat Claude Opus 5 on ARC-AGI-3 using two API settings.
GPT-5.6 Sol only managed 7.8 percent in the standard environment, which discards internal reasoning after each action and used an older interface lacking newer Claude API features.
When tested with OpenAI's own Responses API, including "Retained Reasoning" and smart context "Compaction," the model jumped to 38.3 percent and beat Opus 5 at 30.2 percent.
ARC Prize co-founder Francois Chollet then allowed general, publicly available API settings.
API problems also prevented Argon from completing all 55 games in the Standard Harness, according to the testers.
At low reasoning, the system finished 42 games (49.8 percent), at medium 46 games (46.3 percent).

The Boeing spokesperson explained that the company “stands ready to support” its German customer on next steps.

items.title: Team digitally traces Polish Revolutionary War hero’s West Point contributions
items.originalTitle: Team digitally traces Polish Revolutionary War hero’s West Point contributions
items.summary: The three-man team traveled from Kościuszko’s native Poland to use 3D scanning, aerial photography and other digital technology to digitally document Revolutionary War-era sites and artifacts associated with the Polish-American hero, according to West Point . For his part, Pajor used his background in professional photography to document the sites with multimedia and gigapixel imagery, which will eventually support virtual walkthroughs of the historic site. evidenceRecords.text: The three-man team traveled from Kościuszko’s native Poland to use 3D scanning, aerial photography and other digital technology to digitally document Revolutionary War-era sites and artifacts associated with the Polish-American hero, according to West Point .

As West Point’s earthwork fortifications and landscapes face continual erosion, the project, titled “Tadeusz Kościuszko at West Point: The Digital Heritage of the Polish-American Hero of Freedom,” seeks to preserve the physical traces of the Polish Revolutionary War hero’s contribution to buttressing West Point from the invading British forces.

From Sept. 14 to 29, the Polish team comprising Piotr Bialobrzycki, Damian Kuc and Jerzy Pajo worked to create “3D digital records of the sites as they exist today,” with the project providing “a benchmark for future conservation while eventually allowing people around the world to virtually explore historic resources at West Point… [and] create a precise and lasting digital record of Kościuszko’s material heritage at West Point,” a news release reads.

Project director Bialobrzycki led the terrestrial laser scanning of eight heritage sites at West Point, while Kuc, “the project’s lead specialist in 3D scanning and modeling, used structured-light scanning to document cannons, commemorative plaques, elements of the Kościuszko Monument, the Great Chain and selected artifacts, including Kościuszko’s sword at the West Point Museum,” according to West Point.

For his part, Pajor used his background in professional photography to document the sites with multimedia and gigapixel imagery, which will eventually support virtual walkthroughs of the historic site.
“We wanted to use this moment to demonstrate that the Polish contribution to the American Revolution was concrete and consequential,” Bialobrzycki said.

“Its traces can still be read in the terrain, fortifications, monuments, documents and historical objects at West Point.” Kościuszko’s journey from Polish tutor to war hero was non sequitur — all thanks to an unsuccessful attempt to elope with a lord’s daughter back in Poland.
After discovering his brother had spent all the family’s inheritance, Kościuszko was hired to tutor Louise Sosnowska, a wealthy lord’s daughter.
The pair fell in love and attempted to elope in the fall of 1775 after Lord Sosnowski refused Kosciuszko’s request.

items.title: Google Demonstrates Method to Cut Errors in Quantum Computing’s ‘Magic States’
items.originalTitle: Google Demonstrates Method to Cut Errors in Quantum Computing’s ‘Magic States’
items.summary: Insider Brief Google demonstrated magic-state cultivation on its Willow quantum processor, reducing state-preparation errors about 40-fold and reporting 99.99% logical fidelity, potentially lowering resource demands for error-corrected computing. The team used reinforcement learning to improve processor calibration and developed a measurement technique to avoid overstating the prepared states’ quality.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Google demonstrated magic-state cultivation on its Willow quantum processor, reducing state-preparation errors about 40-fold and reporting 99.99% logical fidelity, potentially lowering resource demands for error-corrected computing.
The team used reinforcement learning to improve processor calibration and developed a measurement technique to avoid overstating the prepared states’ quality.

Researchers transferred prepared states between two error-correcting codes, but larger demonstrations remain necessary, and a storage test produced errors about seven times higher than simulations predicted.
Google researchers reduced errors in a crucial quantum computing resource about 40-fold, demonstrating a method that could lower the hardware demands of useful, error-corrected machines.

The experiment, published in Science , showed that a technique called magic-state cultivation works on Google ’s Willow processor , according to a Google Quantum AI blog post written by Emma Rosenfeld, research scientist and Craig Gidney, quantum software engineer.
The team reported producing states known as T-states with a logical fidelity of 99.99%, which is a measure of how closely a protected quantum state matches its intended form.
The result addresses a problem in quantum computing that preparing these states could consume much of a future machine’s resources and leave less capacity for the calculations it is meant to perform.
Google ’s demonstration moves a proposed way to reduce that burden from theory to hardware.

The researchers were also able to transfer these prepared states between two forms of quantum error correction as an early test of whether the preparation method can connect with the architecture intended to support larger computations.
The work does not necessarily establish that the resource problem has been solved at a practical scale.

Ultimately, then, this looks to be an important, incremental advance toward practical quantum computing that demonstrates a way to prepare essential quantum states with fewer errors and potentially lower hardware demands.
According to Google ’s post, some estimates suggest that making magic states could occupy as much as 95% of a quantum computer’s capacity.

items.originalTitle: QuEra Scientists Named Co-Principal Investigators on Three of Nine Teams in DOE’s Quantum Chemistry Program
items.summary: Insider Brief QuEra Computing scientists will serve as co-principal investigators on three of nine teams selected for the US Department of Energy ‘s $37 million Quantum Computing for Computational Chemistry (QC3) program. The projects target high-temperature superconductors, ultra-strong lightweight magnets and hydrogen production, using quantum algorithms and computational methods to address energy-related materials and chemistry challenges.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief QuEra Computing scientists will serve as co-principal investigators on three of nine teams selected for the US Department of Energy ‘s $37 million Quantum Computing for Computational Chemistry (QC3) program.

The projects target high-temperature superconductors, ultra-strong lightweight magnets and hydrogen production, using quantum algorithms and computational methods to address energy-related materials and chemistry challenges.

QuEra will contribute neutral-atom quantum hardware access and expertise in algorithm and architecture co-design, with the three-year program aiming to demonstrate major improvements over classical methods at approximately 100 logical qubits.

PRESS RELEASE — QuEra Computing , the leader in quantum computing, today announced that its scientists will work with three of the nine teams selected for the Quantum Computing for Computational Chemistry (QC3) program at the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Energy (ARPA-E) to develop neutral-atom based modeling frameworks for complex materials and molecules.
The three-year program, announced by the Department of Energy in March 2026, directs $37 million across the program performers.
ARPA-E’s premise is that the gap closes through full-stack co-design, where improvements of two to three times at each layer of the stack compound into an order of magnitude overall.

The program asks its teams to identify an application worth a quadrillion BTU of energy or a gigaton of CO₂-equivalent, and to pursue a scalable hundredfold improvement over classical state of the art, validated at approximately 100 logical qubits.
The Three Projects QuEra scientists serve as co-principal investigators on each of the following teams, contributing neutral-atom access, expertise, algorithm and architecture co-design.

Superconductor search through Krylov-inspired quantum algorithms, aimed at deepening understanding of high-temperature superconductors and accelerating the discovery of new superconducting materials by co-designing algorithms and error-correction protocols for hardware with reconfigurable connectivity.

items.title: In ‘Quantum 101’ Session, WTO Trade Officials Hear Quantum Encryption Window May Close Within Five Years
items.originalTitle: In ‘Quantum 101’ Session, WTO Trade Officials Hear Quantum Encryption Window May Close Within Five Years
items.summary: Insider Brief A “Quantum 101” session at the World Trade Organization, co-organized by the permanent missions of Israel, Singapore and Switzerland, introduced trade negotiators to quantum technologies and their implications for trade. Speakers from industry, academia and national programs said the most direct link between quantum and trade is encryption, which secures payments, letters of credit, customs filings and e-signatures.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief A “Quantum 101” session at the World Trade Organization, co-organized by the permanent missions of Israel, Singapore and Switzerland, introduced trade negotiators to quantum technologies and their implications for trade.
Speakers from industry, academia and national programs said the most direct link between quantum and trade is encryption, which secures payments, letters of credit, customs filings and e-signatures.
Panelists also pointed to concentrated supply chains, diverging standards and a possible “quantum divide” between countries as trade questions that are already emerging.

The World Trade Organization’s (WTO) member delegations were told this week that the encryption underpinning international trade could be broken by quantum computers within roughly five years, and that the trading system has no shared definition yet of what it means to be “quantum safe.” The warning came at a one-hour session in Geneva, organized by the permanent missions of Israel, Singapore and Switzerland to the WTO.

“We are not here to ask whether the WTO needs rules on quantum technologies,” Carolinn Hjalmroth, head of Israel’s Trade and Economic Mission to the WTO, Foreign Trade Administration , Ministry of Economy and Industry, told the room, adding, “We simply want to start to understand what is changing, what is realistic and what may matter for our economies.” Trade Runs on Encryption Miriam Shtilman-Lavsovski , a partner at Tal Ventures , gave the introductory talk before turning to the issue she framed as most important for trade.
“Trade runs on trust and trust runs on encryption,” Shtilman-Lavsovski, said.

It’s e signatures, letters of credit, customs, payment, etc.” She told delegates that the window for this is probably not more than five years and warned that “harvest now, decrypt later” collection means data sent today is already exposed to a future quantum computer.

She said more than $60 billion in government spending on quantum has been confirmed, with 75% of it coming from five countries, and that private investors have put about $18 billion into quantum startups, 78% of it in five countries.

evidenceRecords.text: AeroVironment, Inc., a global defense technology leader, and Thunder Tiger Corp., a Taiwan-based developer and manufacturer of unmanned systems, today announced a memorandum of understanding to explore collaboration on uncrewed systems integration, potential unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) localization and co-production and future capability co-development in Taiwan.

AeroVironment press release The agreement establishes a framework for evaluating multiple areas of cooperation, including the potential integration of select AV Switchblade Family of Systems configurations with Thunder Tiger’s unmanned surface and ground platforms.
The companies will also explore opportunities to leverage Taiwan’s industrial capacity to support future unmanned aircraft co-production and co-development.
The companies formally signed the memorandum of understanding during the Association of the United States Army Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, D.C.

“Our focus is on bringing proven technology and industrial capabilities together to create more options for how unmanned systems are developed, integrated and produced.” Under the agreement, AV and Thunder Tiger intend to evaluate the technical feasibility of integrating a launcher designed to carry multiple Switchblade all-up rounds with Thunder Tiger’s unmanned surface vessel, including opportunities to advance interoperability and support future demonstrations.

The collaboration reflects AV’s broader approach to create and expand international industrial partnerships and explore opportunities to accelerate the development, integration and production of uncrewed systems. – End –

items.title: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
items.originalTitle: Elorian’s first AI model wants to reason with images, not just about them
items.summary: Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory. Glimpse keeps going back to the source. Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw. Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning. It couldn’t say.

evidenceRecords.text: Most multimodal models look at an image once, convert it to tokens, and then reason about it in text — like describing a photo from memory.
Glimpse keeps going back to the source.

Mid-reasoning, it can crop into a region, pull specific frames from a video, or run code to measure or compare what it’s looking at, a mechanism Elorian calls a “visual scratch space.” Think of someone pinching to zoom on a phone photo to double-check what they thought they saw.
Last year he photographed a board game he’d just finished with friends and asked a frontier model who was winning.
It couldn’t say.

Board games “each have their own visual language, each have their own iconography, symbols,” he told TechCrunch. “To an adult, it’s quite easy to understand what’s going on with minimal text, but these models aren’t able to intuit what the symbols mean.”
“Humans can look at Ikea diagrams, with no text, and assemble Ikea furniture, right?
Why can’t AI models?” he said.
The approach isn’t completely new — OpenAI added crop-and-zoom during reasoning to its o-series models in 2025 — but Elorian’s pitch is that it built the whole model around it, cheaply.
The company says a small team trained Glimpse on a few hundred GPUs and that the model is substantially smaller than the frontier systems it’s benchmarked against.
Glimpse costs $0.60 per million tokens in and $3 per million tokens out — cheaper than mid-level models like Sonnet and Sol but more expensive than lightweight models like Haiku and Luna.
But according to Elorian’s evaluations, Glimpse outperforms even GPT-6 Astra on scientific chart reasoning and short-form video captioning, with competitive results on other visual reasoning tasks.
Longer term, Elorian wants to move from seeing to doing.

The expanded agreement builds on a technical collaboration launched in 2024, when the companies integrated Fortem’s DroneHunter autonomous interceptor into MBDA’s Sky Warden counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS) architecture.

The expanded agreement builds on a technical collaboration launched in 2024, when the companies integrated Fortem’s DroneHunter autonomous interceptor into MBDA’s Sky Warden counter-uncrewed aircraft systems (C-UAS) architecture.
Now, MBDA will offer DroneHunter to its customers, allowing them to add the interceptor to their existing air defense networks instead of deploying an entirely separate system.
Sales will remain subject to applicable export authorizations.

The companies are also jointly offering FireThorn, an autonomous interceptor they developed together to counter one-way attack drones and other hostile uncrewed aircraft, including Shahed/Geran and Orlan platforms.
The two systems offer different approaches to dealing with aerial threats.
DroneHunter uses a net to capture hostile drones, making it an option for environments where minimizing collateral damage matters or where operators want to recover a drone intact for evidence.
FireThorn, meanwhile, is designed for more demanding engagements, using Fortem’s high-speed, radar-guided autonomous airframe and an MBDA NATO-approved warhead to destroy its target.
“Militaries don’t need another standalone gadget.
They need autonomous interceptors that plug into the architecture they already trust,” Fortem Technologies CEO Jon Gruen said in announcing the expanded partnership.
Gruen added that working with MBDA gives allied forces a faster route to protecting troops, military bases and critical infrastructure.
The partnership reflects a broader challenge facing modern air defenses: dealing with the growing use of relatively inexpensive drones for reconnaissance and attacks.

NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries.
Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”.
As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November.
In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”.
The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”.
In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus”.
British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”.
The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”.
Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region.
As a work of cinema, it is exemplary.
As a work of journalism, it is inarguable.
As a document, it is an indictment.”
The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”.

The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”.

items.originalTitle: Germany Publishes National Post-Quantum Cryptography Migration Guideline
items.summary: Insider Brief Germany’s BMI, BMDS and BSI have published a national guideline for implementing the EU roadmap for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). The guideline recommends completing migrations for high-risk systems by the end of 2030 at the latest and largely completing the broader transition by 2035. evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Germany’s BMI, BMDS and BSI have published a national guideline for implementing the EU roadmap for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC).
The guideline recommends completing migrations for high-risk systems by the end of 2030 at the latest and largely completing the broader transition by 2035.
The recommendations call for clear migration responsibilities and deadlines, systematic quantum-risk assessments, early coordination with manufacturers and supply chains, and cryptographic agility.
PRESS RELEASE — Quantum computers pose an increasingly real threat to the security of cryptographic methods and thus to cybersecurity itself.

The Federal Ministry of the Interior (BMI), the Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs and State Modernization (BMDS) and the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) are now jointly publishing the Guideline for the implementation of the EU Roadmap on Post-Quantum Cryptography for Germany.
It stems from an initiative by EU member states that had put forward recommendations for an EU-wide coordinated transition to quantum-safe cryptography, so-called post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

Objectives of the Guideline The national guideline is aimed particularly at federal, state and local governments, as well as organizations and companies, including operators of critical infrastructure.

It provides structured recommendations for the transition to quantum-safe cryptography and confirms the timelines of the European Roadmap: high-risk use cases should be switched to quantum-safe methods as early as possible; for these systems, the migration should be completed by the end of 2030 at the latest.

The measures recommended in the national guideline include, in particular, the establishment of clear responsibilities and binding deadlines for the transition, the consideration of post-quantum cryptography in accordance with the state of the art, the systematic assessment of quantum risk and its anchoring in risk management, and the early involvement of manufacturers and supply chains.

The guideline creates BMI, BMDS and BSIa basis for the coordinated transition to quantum-safe cryptography in Germany and provide public and private actors with a framework for the upcoming steps of this transition.
Source: Transition to post-quantum cryptography: Guideline on the national implementation of the EU roadmap published

evidenceRecords.text: Typically a country may host a U.S. Army Civil Affairs team or two — the Army’s special operations forces contingent that connects military forces with civilian populations — but Panama is home to an entire U.S. Civil Affairs company, White said, that works in virtually every district.
The U.S. has military salvage dive teams operating around the canal and cross-training with Panamanian forces.
Military doctors work alongside Panamanian medical professionals to assist local populations, performing colonoscopies and cataract surgeries.
White said one of the lessons the U.S. learned during its decades-long wars in Iraq and Afghanistan was that the military cannot quickly create trust.

“And so, being here — present — doing things on the regular with SENAFRONT and SENAN, with the government of Panama — and with their permission to do it — it helps build that trust.” Though Panama does not have a standing Army, SENAFRONT and SENAN are two branches of the Panamanian Public Forces.
Those teams, he said, identify gaps in civilian infrastructure, such as dilapidated schools or unsafe bridges.
Engineer soldiers rotate through the country, building out structures for jungle students.
Dentists and optometrists — even veterinarians — rotate through rural parts of the country.

“In a crisis, you simply can’t surge trust,” he said. “And so, being here — present — doing things on the regular with SENAFRONT and SENAN, with the government of Panama — and with their permission to do it — it helps build that trust.” Though Panama does not have a standing Army, SENAFRONT and SENAN are two branches of the Panamanian Public Forces.
With terrain different from the U.S.’s Hawaii jungle course, Panama’s environment replicates other jungle biomes where the U.S. may find itself in conflict.
The Western Hemisphere, White said, abounds with jungle landscape.
Officials have been adamant that the future does not hold permanent military basing for U.S. troops.
White said the U.S. contingent works to uphold the Neutrality Treaty of 1977 — which guarantees the Panama Canal remains neutral and open for ships of all nations to transit peacefully.

Developed from research led by Stony Brook physicist Eden Figueroa and his former graduate students, Qu-MEM systems are being deployed on quantum networking testbeds in New York and Europe.
PRESS RELEASE — A quantum technology invented at the State University of New York (SUNY) at Stony Brook (Stony Brook University) is earning international recognition.

Qunnect ’s Qu-MEM, a commercial room-temperature quantum memory device developed from Stony Brook-patented technology, has been named to TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 in the Experimental category for concept inventions and prototypes showing future potential.
This recognition highlights Stony Brook’s role in advancing quantum technology and demonstrates how university research can move beyond the laboratory to help shape emerging industries.

Qunnect ’s Qu-MEM grew out of research led by Professor Eden Figueroa, Stony Brook’s Endowed Presidential Professor of Physics and director of the Stony Brook University Quantum Institute alongside alumni/graduate students Mehdi Namazi, PhD ’18, and Mael Flament, MS ’19.
Qu-MEM is the world’s first commercial room-temperature quantum memory device, currently expanding Stony Brook’s SCY-QNET, America’s largest quantum internet.

King Jr. said, “The State University of New York at Stony Brook has emerged as a global leader in quantum technology and research through the strong investment by Governor Hochul, state leaders, and SUNY, and thanks to world-class researchers, faculty, and students who are moving this field forward.

I applaud the State University of New York at Stony Brook on this well-earned recognition, which reinforces that investments made in SUNY research help move our state and society forward.” “ Stony Brook University is proud to celebrate Qunnect ’s recognition by TIME for creating one of the year’s best inventions.

This quantum memory is an essential component in Stony Brook’s fiber and wireless quantum network, which is the largest metropolitan area quantum network in the world communicating quantum information via entangled photons.

This quantum network, which we plan to grow first to upstate New York and then throughout the country, is capable of protecting sensitive data in critical sectors including healthcare, finance and national defense,” said Stony Brook University President Andrea Goldsmith.

items.summary: But when the Kendall Square Association gathered local stakeholders for its 18th Annual Meeting Thursday, the conversation focused on innovation primarily in the context of community.
