evidenceRecords.text: But when the Kendall Square Association gathered local stakeholders for its 18th Annual Meeting Thursday, the conversation focused on innovation primarily in the context of community.

The event, which took place at the nonprofit startup incubator The Engine, attracted people from across Cambridge, including business leaders, elected officials, local residents, and students, for a night of local food and conversation about the advance of technologies like artificial intelligence and what they mean for society.

“How can we make AI not an enemy of work, but a tool for workers to expand their capabilities and build new expertise or do new things?” asked MIT Institute Professor Daron Acemoglu in a keynote talk.

“The world is at a point in time where we need new innovations and new adaptations to growing challenges.” Acemoglu’s keynote was one of several presentations at the event, which also featured music from the Kendall Square Orchestra, a vote on new KSA board members, and awards for organizations making a positive impact through innovation.

KSA is a nonprofit made up of over 150 organizations across Kendall Square, from major companies to universities, research organizations, and the independent shops and restaurants that give Kendall Square its distinct character.
“People come to Kendall Square to make the world better,” said KSA Executive Director Beth O’Neill Maloney in her opening remarks.

“It isn’t just the universities or labs, it’s also the culture of collaboration among nonprofits, governments, and residents.” Broad Institute Chief Communications Officer Lee McGuire started his talk by reviewing a 2009 report on what made Kendall Square such a powerful driver of innovation, noting that factors like talent density, education, and a collective voice remain strong in the area today.

“It is the job of the Kendall Square Association and all of us to help protect those things, make sure we name them, understand them, and see them as essential elements of making sure this community stays what it is no matter what happens.

items.title: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
items.originalTitle: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
items.summary: Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures. Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI. Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs.

evidenceRecords.text: Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.

Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5.
It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.
Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs.
Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly.

That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.
The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.

It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage.
In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.

items.title: AI agents get better by anticipating errors in their own software changes
items.originalTitle: AI agents get better by anticipating errors in their own software changes
items.summary: Some artificial intelligence agents can modify the programs and instructions governing their own work, with the goal of improving performance. These changes, however, can introduce errors, while testing unsuccessful modifications consumes resources. Researchers at the University of Virginia, Microsoft Research and Tsinghua University recently developed forecasting software that helps AI agents anticipate the consequences of proposed edits before testing the modified software.

evidenceRecords.text: Some artificial intelligence agents can modify the programs and instructions governing their own work, with the goal of improving performance.
These changes, however, can introduce errors, while testing unsuccessful modifications consumes resources.

Researchers at the University of Virginia, Microsoft Research and Tsinghua University recently developed forecasting software that helps AI agents anticipate the consequences of proposed edits before testing the modified software.

The approach, introduced in an article posted to the arXiv preprint server, was evaluated on programming tasks, predicting whether scientific papers would be accepted for publication, designing rewards for simulated robots and grading advanced mathematical solutions.
Initial results suggest that using forecasts to guide software changes helped agents improve more efficiently.
The researchers' approach builds on HyperAgents, a framework combining two AI components or agents.
The first performs tasks, while the second modifies the code and instructions used by both.
Earlier versions and their results are preserved in an archive to inform subsequent changes.
The team introduced a new component called the Improvement Dynamics Model, which examines a proposed modification, the agent being modified and earlier results.
It also predicts outcomes for individual tasks, distinguishing between incorrect answers and attempts that never finish.
Distinguishing between incorrect answers and unfinished attempts is valuable, as the two can require different interventions.
An incorrect answer may require better reasoning, while an unfinished attempt could indicate that the software needs fixing.
Instead, they suggest that forecasting can help agents identify helpful software changes, and that experience predicting these changes could assist improvement on a different task.

The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday. He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state. The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).

evidenceRecords.text: Ethiopia has announced that an interim government will take control of the state of Tigray, after its armed forces retook control of the northern region.
The installation of the six-month administration was announced in a statement by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday.
He pledged that free elections would then be held in the state.
The move comes after the Ethiopian military pushed back an uprising launched last month by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF).
Tigray’s main political party had launched the insurrection after announcing in April that it was retaking control of the region, effectively ending a peace deal with Ethiopia’s federal government.
The government promised that the interim government would create “a stable political situation” in Tigray so that free elections could be held.
It has appointed five officials to run the state, including the mayor of the capital, Mekelle.
The TPLF governed Ethiopia for nearly 30 years until 2018, when Abiy’s party came to power.
Tigray, in response, boycotted national elections and rejected the central government, creating a severe rift.

items.title: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
items.originalTitle: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
items.summary: El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific. Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.

evidenceRecords.text: 6 Min Read NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño This visualization compares three ocean data products, sea surface temperature anomaly, apparent visible wavelength, and sea surface height anomaly, over the same months in 2025 and 2026.
Credits: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific.
NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
“Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
Credit: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño.
Credit: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio El Niño’s warm waters also change the color of the ocean.
One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific.
Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long.
Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific.
The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise.

The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more.
The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm.
Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters).

Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software.

At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.

He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste.

“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.

“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”

Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets.
By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon.
You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding.
We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things.
“But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.

evidenceRecords.text: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.

Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

A leading theory is that the aviator, who broke several records including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image.

items.title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.originalTitle: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.summary: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

evidenceRecords.text: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally.
On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009.
His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.

After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.
The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".
After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand.

items.title: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
items.originalTitle: Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs
items.summary: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs. The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday. Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers.

evidenceRecords.text: Meta has launched what it calls the “most capable” open-weight model in the United States.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.
Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor.
It has also been designed to run locally on Apple’s computers.
However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget.
The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.
Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks.

Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included “bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.”
The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.
Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren’t afforded by closed and proprietary models.
Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don’t allow.
